As of 315 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Well above normal temperatures with mostly dry 
conditions are expected through Friday. Record breaking highs are 
possible Wednesday. 

Sunny skies and warm (for mid-October) temperatures are ongoing 
across our forecast area this afternoon. Rising heights are noted in 
the mid and upper levels, with high pressure centered south of the 
area at the surface. A weak shortwave slides through overnight, but 
this feature will not have any noticeable impact on the local 
weather. Overnight lows continue the mild trend...generally in the 
lower to mid 60s. 

The peak in the heat is still expected on Wednesday, with high 
confidence in record-breaking temperatures for most of the area. 
This will occur as the ridge axis aloft shifts eastward from the 
TN/OH Valleys. Highs at least in the upper 80s are almost a given, 
and a blend of the various hi-res and statistical guidance yields 
highs of 90-92 F for most areas W of the Chesapeake Bay. As 
noted by the previous shift, the statistical guidance remains a 
few degrees higher than the NBM, so there certainly is some 
room for temps to overperform some. Regardless, highs should be
well into record territory with daily records only in the mid 
to upper 80s. See climate section below for site-specific data.
While these temperatures resemble mid-summmer values, dew 
points in the lower to mid 60s should suppress the "mugginess" 
factor.

A cold front will approach the region from the N Wednesday night and 
is forecast to drop through the local area Thursday morning. 
Transient high pressure will also set up over interior New England, 
so a brief wedge-like pattern is possible during most of the day 
with onshore flow and cool/cloudy skies. With increasing confidence 
in the frontal passage occuring before peak heating, have lowered 
highs ~2-4 degrees compared to the previous forecast and the NBM. 
This is more in line with most of the traditional model guidance and 
ultimately would not be surprised if temps trend even cooler. Exact 
timing of temps remains a challenge due the the frontal passage, but 
daytime highs are likely to be achieved on the earlier side and 
range from the 70s/lower 80s S to 60s across the northern tier. 
Clouds will also thicken from N to S Thursday as the front drops 
south. In addition, some weak isentropic lift/overrunning north
of the front could result in generally light rain across the 
northern third of the area Thursday. QPF is on the order of a 
few hundredths of an inch. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front crosses the area Friday evening, 
with gusty winds expected ahead of and behind the front. A few 
showers and storms are also possible in the afternoon and evening 
hours of Friday. 

A deep upper trough is forecast to dig across the Great Lakes 
Thursday night into Friday with a strengthening surface low over the 
Ohio Valley. This will quickly erode any wedge-like airmass and 
allow a quick transition back to deep-layer S/SW flow as the front 
lifts back N as a warm front. High temps rebound into the upper 70s 
to low 80s N with mid and upper 80s S. It will become breezy out of 
the SW by Friday afternoon, with gusts to 30-35 mph possible. 
Scattered showers are also probable ahead of an associated strong 
cold front, particularly across N and NE portions of the local area. 
An embedded storm or two is also possible but this is dependent
on the degree of available instability. Any shower/storm could 
mix down locally higher wind gusts and a Marginal (level 1/5) 
severe risk may eventually be needed, per SPC. 

Rapidly deepening low pressure will translate from the Great Lakes 
into the New England region by Friday night, with the aforementioned 
sharp/strong cold front extending southwestward. This front will 
cross the local area Friday evening into early Saturday with 
significant cold advection moving into the region. Some additional 
precip is possible along and ahead of the frontal passage through 
midnight, mainly over the eastern half of the area. QPF does not 
look nearly as impressive as a front of this strength would suggest, 
mainly due to the unfavorable trough orientation and disconnect from 
any appreciable moisture sources. However, gusty winds are likely to 
continue into the Friday overnight period and could reach 35-40 mph 
immediately along and behind the front. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Much cooler temperatures arrive this weekend. Frost 
is possible across inland portions of the area. 

Strong (1035mb+) high pressure builds into the region behind the 
front with upper troughing remaining over the eastern CONUS, 
resulting in well below normal temperatures this weekend. Afternoon 
highs on Saturday likely struggle to get out of the 50s across the 
northern half of the CWA despite mostly sunny skies. Low 60s are
